summary:
Footprints in Space is an interactive educational website that explores NASA's equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. It aims to bring attention to the machines that played important roles in space exploration but are often overlooked once their missions end.

The website allows visitors to explore different pieces of equipment, learn about their original purposes, follow their mission journeys and discover the scientific contributions they made. Through interactive planetary maps, mission timelines, photographs and equipment profiles, users can understand where these machines remain and why they were left behind.

It also includes educational activities and quizzes to make learning about space exploration more engaging, particularly for younger audiences.

By bringing together NASA data, mission archives and storytelling, Footprints in Space connects past missions with the future of space exploration. Its goal is to show that even when a machine's mission comes to an end, its discoveries and contributions remain valuable to science.
details:
Footprints in Space

Footprints in Space is an interactive digital museum developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project explores the equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars, telling the stories of the machines that helped us understand other worlds. Rather than treating these machines as forgotten objects, we wanted to show why they were sent into space, what they achieved and how they contributed to scientific discoveries.

The website is divided into several sections, each focusing on a different aspect of space exploration. The Equipment Archive features 15 documented lunar and Martian machines, with individual pages covering their purpose, engineering, achievements, locations and current status. Visitors can also explore an interactive planetary map with 2D and 3D views, showing where different missions landed. The Mission Timeline presents important events in the history of these missions, while the Discoveries section explains what scientists learned from the equipment. We also included an Explorer's Corner with quizzes, matching games and challenges to make learning more engaging. Finally, the Sources page brings together official NASA archives and includes a live search feature connected to NASA's public Image and Video Library.

One of the main benefits of Footprints in Space is that it brings information from different NASA resources together in one place. Instead of searching through separate documents and websites, visitors can explore mission details, photographs, coordinates and scientific findings through a single platform. The interactive activities also allow users to test their knowledge and learn at their own pace. We hope the project encourages students and young space enthusiasts to become more interested in astronomy, science and aerospace engineering.

A feature that makes the project particularly interesting is The Last Signal, which explores how certain missions came to an end. We wanted to tell these stories in a way that was engaging without compromising historical accuracy, so we used verified mission information rather than fictional final messages. More broadly, the website connects equipment, locations, timelines and discoveries, allowing visitors to understand how individual machines contributed to our knowledge of the Moon and Mars.

The website was developed using TypeScript, HTML, CSS and React 19, with Vite and Tailwind CSS for development and styling. React Router manages the different webpages, while Three.js powers the interactive 3D maps. We also used SVG diagrams for scientific illustrations and Lucide React for icons. Our information was gathered and checked against NASA resources, including NSSDCA, the Planetary Data System and Solar System Treks. The website also uses NASA's public Image and Video Library API to retrieve photographs. LocalStorage allows visitors to save their quiz and game progress in their browsers.

Throughout development, we focused on scientific accuracy, accessibility and performance. Mission dates, locations and discoveries were checked against official sources, and we made sure to distinguish between equipment that was intentionally left behind, retired equipment and machines that are still operational. We also wanted the website to work across different devices, so its layout adapts to desktops, tablets and mobile phones. Since the 3D map may not work smoothly on every device, we included a 2D alternative.

Ultimately, Footprints in Space aims to change how people think about the equipment left behind on other worlds. These machines are more than just abandoned hardware; they represent years of engineering, exploration and scientific progress. Through this project, we hope to make their stories easier to discover and inspire more people to appreciate the role they have played in expanding our understanding of the universe.
